task_brief: Day 3 of "Foundations Project and Impact Review" (unit 6, grade 9) is a guided practice on test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Deliver a foundations software project with version history, test evidence, an accessibility audit, and a privacy and security review. Today's work contributes to that by handling test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification at the guided practice stage, against the unit's wider topics of project scoping and success criteria, version control and iterative build history, test evidence and defect closure, and accessibility verification. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Complete two supported problems on test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification. On the first, work step by step with prompts available, and after each step write the one-line reason that step is correct. On the second, work without prompts and only check the reference after you commit to an answer. Both problems must show the intermediate states — a trace table, printed values, or a labelled diagram — not just a final result. Then state which of the two felt less certain and name the specific step where your confidence dropped. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification, and it belongs to "Foundations Project and Impact Review", which also covers separate topics such as project scoping and success criteria. Close out with this check before you stop: Show your reasoning on the faded example of test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification and identify the check that confirms it. At grade 9 the bar is independent work with explicit criteria set before you start, and evidence that you evaluated the finished result against those criteria rather than against how it felt.

guided_scaffold_note: Scaffolding for test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification fades within the session: the first case may be worked with the reference, model, or prompts in view, and the second must be attempted before checking anything. The supporting adult may ask "what supports that move?" after a step but should not supply the step. Where the unscaffolded attempt diverges from the scaffolded one, the divergence itself is the thing to examine, not something to erase.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.
Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, diagrammed, or demonstrated responses; where code is the target, accept pseudocode, block-based, or annotated-trace evidence.
Provide screen-reader-compatible editors, adjustable font and contrast, keyboard-only workflows, and an offline paper-and-trace route for every programming task.
task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on test evidence and defect closure and accessibility verification rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
